title: The Kalam and contingency arguments: why is there something rather than nothing?
claim: Two related arguments. The Kalam runs: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause, and that cause lies beyond space, time and matter. The second premise has scientific support. The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem (2003) shows that any universe expanding on average cannot be past-eternal in classical spacetime. Vilenkin: 'With the proof now in place, cosmologists can no longer hide behind the possibility of a past-eternal universe. There is no escape: they have to face the problem of a cosmic beginning.' Quote him precisely, though. He also says plainly that this is not a proof of God, and that it gives 'not much of an advantage to the theologian over the scientist.' The Leibnizian contingency argument does not even need a beginning. An eternal universe would still be a contingent thing, and its existence would still call for an explanation outside itself. Both arguments make theism a serious metaphysical contender. Neither makes it a leap in the dark.

sources.name: SEP, 'Cosmological Argument' (Reichenbach)
Borde, Guth & Vilenkin, 'Inflationary spacetimes are not past-complete' (2003)
William Lane Craig, Reasonable Faith (Kalam materials)
Sean Carroll, Preposterous Universe (post-Craig-debate reflections)
Wikipedia, 'Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem'

response: Graham Oppy answers that the causal premise is an extrapolation. We take what we see inside the universe and apply it to the universe itself, a domain where we have exactly zero examples. Quantum mechanics already strains the rule that every beginning has a cause, since some events look indeterministic — though the quantum vacuum is admittedly not 'nothing'. The naturalist can simply call the initial physical state necessary, or brute. That is the same stopping move the theist makes with God, and it posits one entity fewer. Sean Carroll adds a physics point. The BGV theorem is about classical spacetime. It says classical descriptions break down, not that reality began. Quantum-gravity models such as Aguirre-Gratton evade it, and Vilenkin himself denies that it carries theological force. Both explanations stop somewhere. Theism has not shown that its stopping point is the better one.
rationale: Genuinely open — and saying so is the credibility move. The facts are real: BGV is a published theorem, and the contingency question is a serious one. The metaphysics is contested by the best philosophers on both sides. So present it as this: theism is a rationally serious answer to the deepest question there is. Never present it as a knockdown. And never misquote Vilenkin. He is abused by both sides, and a skeptic who has read him will check.

plain.d: The Kalam runs like this. Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began. So the universe has a cause, and it sits outside space and time. The contingency argument, from Leibniz, needs no beginning at all. Even an endless universe could have failed to be there. So why is there one?

In 2003 three physicists proved a theorem: Borde, Guth and Vilenkin. Any universe that expands on average cannot be endless in the past. Vilenkin put it bluntly. He wrote that cosmologists "can no longer hide behind the possibility of a past-eternal universe."

plain.t: Quote him fairly, or not at all
plain.d: Vilenkin also says his theorem is not a proof of God. He says it gives "not much of an advantage to the theologian over the scientist." Say that part yourself, first. Someone who has read him will check.

Graham Oppy is an atheist thinker. He says we have no example of a thing beginning outside the universe. So the rule about causes may not reach that far. Sean Carroll adds a physics point. The theorem is about classical spacetime. Quantum gravity models get round it, such as Aguirre-Gratton. And the atheist can call the first physical state necessary. That is the same stopping move you make with God, with one thing fewer.

Contested, and say so. The facts are real. What they mean is argued over by good thinkers on both sides. Use it like this. God is a serious answer to the deepest question there is. Never as a knockdown.
"Why is there anything at all? I don't think that question has a cheap answer."

title: Fine-tuning: the constants of physics are set on a knife's edge
claim: The constants and starting conditions of the universe fall within staggeringly narrow life-permitting ranges. The cosmological constant is tuned to roughly 1 part in 10^120. Roger Penrose put the precision of the universe's low-entropy start at 1 in 10^10^123. That is a number with more zeroes in it than there are particles in the visible universe. This is not a creationist talking point. The data is granted by physicists who are not theists. Fred Hoyle was an atheist when he wrote it: 'A common sense interpretation of the facts suggests that a superintellect has monkeyed with physics, as well as with chemistry and biology.' Martin Rees built a book around six such numbers. The theist argument is that design explains this better than brute chance does. Of all the arguments for God, this one gets the most respect from working scientists. It also leans least on contested metaphysics.

sources.name: SEP, 'Fine-Tuning' (Friederich)
Wikipedia, 'Fine-tuned universe' (Penrose, Rees, Hoyle citations)
Roger Penrose, The Road to Reality (initial entropy calculation)
Luke Barnes & Geraint Lewis, A Fortunate Universe (CUP)
Sean Carroll, 'Does the Universe Need God?'

response: The multiverse, plus anthropic selection. If vast numbers of universes exist with varied constants, observers must find themselves in a life-permitting one. No tuner is needed. And inflation gives the multiverse its own support. Sean Carroll presses further. We have no way to measure how likely a constant is, so 'improbable' may not even be defined here. And under theism, why would God need tuned physics at all? An all-powerful being could sustain life in any universe. On that reading, tuning is arguably evidence that life arose by natural means. The theist reply has force. The multiverse generator would itself need tuned laws, and anthropic reasoning is plagued by Boltzmann-brain predictions. But that reply reopens the debate rather than closing it.
rationale: The strongest of the existence arguments. The data is uncontested. The design inference is taken seriously in peer-reviewed philosophy of physics by Luke Barnes and Geraint Lewis. But the multiverse is a genuine rival, not a dodge, even though it faces its own regress. Grade it contested, leaning strong. Lead with the numbers and with the witnesses who are not theists: Hoyle, Penrose, Rees. Then grant that the multiverse is a serious rival. Note that it too posits things beyond the evidence, and that we cannot see them either. Let the skeptic feel the symmetry.

plain.d: Physics has constants that are not derived from anything. Change some of them slightly and no stars form. No chemistry. No universe that lasts. The cosmological constant sits at about 1 part in 10^120 of its natural value.

This is not a creationist talking point. Fred Hoyle was an atheist when he wrote it: "A common sense interpretation of the facts suggests that a superintellect has monkeyed with physics." Roger Penrose put the odds of the universe's low-entropy start at 1 in 10^10^123. Martin Rees built a book around six such numbers.

The multiverse. If huge numbers of universes exist with different constants, life can only turn up in a fit one. No tuner needed. Inflation gives that idea its own support. Sean Carroll presses harder. We have no way to measure how likely a constant is, so "improbable" may mean nothing here. And why would an all-powerful God need tuned physics at all?
The machine that makes the universes would need tuned laws itself. And this kind of reasoning has a known bug, named after Boltzmann brains. That reopens the debate. It does not close it.

The best of the God arguments, and still contested. The data is not in doubt. Luke Barnes and Geraint Lewis defend the design reading in peer-reviewed work. The multiverse is a real rival, not a dodge. Note that it also posits things we cannot see. Then let the other person feel how alike the two moves are.
"The constants are on a knife's edge. Both our answers go past what we can see. Mine just goes a different way."

title: The moral argument: objective moral facts fit a moral universe
claim: Nearly everyone lives as if some things are really wrong, and that includes nearly every atheist. Torturing children for fun is not a preference violation. It is an abomination, and it would remain one if every human culture approved of it. The moral argument holds that objective, binding moral facts fit far more naturally in a universe grounded in a personal Good than in one of particles and selection pressures. The Euthyphro dilemma deserves its steelman: is a thing good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? If the first, morality is arbitrary. If the second, the standard stands above God. The classical answer is a third option the dilemma omits. The Good is neither above God nor decreed by God. It is God's own necessary nature, and commands are expressions of it. Note carefully what this argument does not say. It does not say atheists are immoral, or that they cannot know right from wrong. Romans 2:14-15 asserts the opposite.

sources.name: SEP, 'Moral Arguments for the Existence of God' (C. S. Evans)
Wikipedia, 'Euthyphro dilemma' (incl. divine-nature responses)
C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, Book I
Erik Wielenberg, Robust Ethics (the strongest non-theist realism)

response: Erik Wielenberg and Graham Oppy grant moral realism entirely and keep God out of it. Basic ethical truths — 'pain is bad', 'cruelty is wrong' — can be metaphysically necessary brute facts that need no ground. That is exactly how the theist treats God's nature: as an ungrounded necessary stopping point. And saying 'God's nature is the Good' merely relocates Euthyphro. Is God's nature good because of the properties it has? Then those properties do the work, and God is dispensable. Or is it good merely because it is God's? Then the arbitrariness returns. Meanwhile J. L. Mackie's other horn waits. Perhaps there are no objective values at all. Our sense of binding obligation may be an evolutionary projection, which is exactly what selection would produce whether or not it tracked any truth.
rationale: Honest grade: contested. The divine-nature answer genuinely dissolves the pop-level Euthyphro. But Wielenberg's non-theistic Platonism is a real rival, and sophisticated skeptics will deploy it. The power of this argument is existential rather than syllogistic. Most people cannot actually live as nihilists, and the argument names why. Never, ever let it slide into 'atheists have no morals'. See the don't-use entry — Scripture itself forbids that move.

plain.d: Almost everyone lives as if some things are really wrong. Torturing children for fun is not a matter of taste. It would still be wrong if every culture on earth approved. The argument is that facts like that fit a universe grounded in a personal Good better than one of particles.

plain.t: The famous objection, and the real answer
plain.d: Euthyphro asks it this way. Is a thing good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? If the first, morals are arbitrary. If the second, the standard sits above God. The classic answer is a third option the question leaves out. The Good is God's own nature. Commands express it.

plain.t: What this argument does not say
plain.d: It does not say atheists are bad people. It does not say they cannot tell right from wrong. Romans 2:14-15 says the opposite. Gentiles without the law "do by nature what the law requires." Scripture itself blocks that move.

Erik Wielenberg keeps moral facts and drops God. Basic truths like "cruelty is wrong" can be necessary brute facts, needing no ground. That is exactly how you treat God's nature. Graham Oppy adds that "God's nature is the Good" only moves the problem. Is that nature good for the traits it has, or good just because it is his? And J. L. Mackie waits on the other side. Perhaps there are no real values, and our sense of duty is an evolved projection.

Contested. The divine-nature answer does kill the popular form of Euthyphro. Wielenberg's version is a real rival. The power of this argument is lived, not logical. Most people cannot actually live as if nothing is wrong.
"Do you think some things would still be wrong even if every person alive approved of them?"

title: The argument from reason: can a mind built by non-rational causes be trusted about ultimate reality?
claim: If naturalism is true, human cognition is the output of non-rational physical causes, selected for survival rather than for truth. Selection cares whether you flee the tiger. It does not care whether your metaphysics is correct. So why trust such a brain when it reasons about quantum cosmology, mathematics, or naturalism itself? C. S. Lewis and Victor Reppert press this as the argument from reason. Alvin Plantinga formalises it as the Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism. Darwin himself worried about it in a letter. The star witness is Thomas Nagel, a serious atheist philosopher. His book Mind and Cosmos is subtitled 'Why the Materialist Neo-Darwinian Conception of Nature Is Almost Certainly False'. He argues that consciousness, cognition and value cannot be accommodated by materialism, and he pointedly declines theism. Add David Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness: subjective experience stubbornly resists reduction to physics. Theism expects minds at the foundation of reality. Materialism must conjure them from what is mindless.

sources.name: Thomas Nagel, Mind and Cosmos (OUP, 2012)
Victor Reppert, C. S. Lewis's Dangerous Idea
SEP, 'Consciousness' (hard problem overview)
Plantinga, Where the Conflict Really Lies (EAAN)

response: The standard reply is strong. Truth-tracking cognition is fitness-enhancing across the domains where cognition evolved, because an animal systematically wrong about its environment dies. Reliability in evolved domains, plus error-correcting institutions such as logic, mathematics and science, bootstraps trustworthy reasoning beyond them. The naturalist need not claim that unaided intuition is reliable about metaphysics. And note that the blade cuts both ways: theistic metaphysics is produced by the same evolved brain. As for consciousness, mysterianism, panpsychism and Nagel's own non-theistic natural teleology are all live options. 'Materialism struggles' does not entail 'therefore a personal God'. Nagel himself, honest to the end, refuses that inference.
rationale: Contested, and Nagel is the right way to present it. Not 'gotcha, atheism refutes itself', but 'even honest atheists see that mind is a deep anomaly for materialism'. Deploy it as a worldview comparison: which picture of reality expects minds to exist? Never deploy it as a claim that atheists cannot reason. They visibly can, and the argument does not say otherwise.

plain.d: If nature is all there is, your brain was built by causes that do not think. Selection cared whether you ran from the tiger. It did not care whether your view of reality was right. So why trust that brain on the deepest questions?

C. S. Lewis and Victor Reppert call it the argument from reason. Alvin Plantinga tightened it into the Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism. Darwin himself worried about it in a letter. The best witness is not a Christian. Thomas Nagel is an atheist thinker. His book Mind and Cosmos carries the subtitle "Why the Materialist Neo-Darwinian Conception of Nature Is Almost Certainly False." He still turns down theism, and says so plainly.

David Chalmers named the hard problem of consciousness. Why is there something it is like to be you? Physics can map the wiring. It does not hand you the experience. Theism expects minds at the base of reality. Materialism has to make minds out of stuff that has none.

Getting the world right does help you survive. An animal badly wrong about its surroundings dies. Reliable senses in daily life, plus logic, maths and science as error-checkers, carry you the rest of the way. And the blade cuts both ways. Your theology comes from the same evolved brain. On consciousness, panpsychism and Nagel's own godless teleology are live options. "Materialism struggles" does not add up to "therefore a personal God."

Contested. Use Nagel's framing, not a gotcha. Honest atheists see that mind is a deep oddity for materialism. Never claim atheists cannot reason. They plainly can, and the argument never said otherwise.
"Which picture of reality would you expect minds to show up in? That's the question I keep landing on."

title: The minimal facts: what even skeptical scholars grant about Easter
claim: Set apart what critical scholarship grants — not what apologists claim. (1) Jesus of Nazareth was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Bart Ehrman calls this one of the most secure facts of ancient history. Tacitus and Josephus attest it. Mythicism is rejected by nearly every trained specialist, the atheist ones included. (2) Soon afterward, his followers had experiences they were sure were appearances of the risen Jesus. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, wrote: 'It may be taken as historically certain that Peter and the disciples had experiences after Jesus's death in which Jesus appeared to them as the risen Christ.' (3) The preaching began in Jerusalem almost at once, and Paul the persecutor and James the skeptical brother both joined. The empty tomb is more disputed, so be honest about it. Gary Habermas's much-cited figure of about 75% of scholars is a survey of published work, not a poll of scholars. Ehrman doubts even the burial by Joseph of Arimathea. The Gospels do make women the ones who find the tomb, and their word carried little legal weight, which still counts in its favour. The granted facts force one question. What best explains them?

sources.name: Gary Habermas, 'Resurrection Research from 1975 to the Present' (JSHJ 2005)
Bart Ehrman on the certainty of the crucifixion
Gerd Lüdemann, What Really Happened to Jesus (1995)
Dale Allison, The Resurrection of Jesus (T&T Clark, 2021) — the judicious middle
N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God

response: Ehrman replies that every granted fact has a natural explanation. Visions of the recently dead are well documented in grief studies. A few sincere visions among shattered followers, read through Jewish hopes about the end, and then retold for decades, yields all that we find. The empty tomb may be a later addition. Mark, our earliest Gospel, ends with no appearance stories. Crucified criminals were routinely left unburied or thrown into common graves. The women-witnesses point assumes the criterion of embarrassment. Recent scholarship treats that as shaky, notably Rafael Rodríguez and the memory-studies school. Women finding a tomb also fits Mark's habit of reversals rather nicely. And sincere changed lives attest conviction, not its cause. The Millerites and the Sabbateans were changed too.
rationale: Admitted — for the facts themselves, which is exactly how to use it. The crucifixion, the disciples' resurrection experiences, the early Jerusalem proclamation, and the conversions of Paul and James are conceded by the field's leading skeptics, in print. The inference from those facts to a risen Jesus is where the real argument lives. Say that out loud and you will be the most credible apologist the skeptic has ever met. Do not cite the 75% empty-tomb statistic without its caveat.

plain.d: It asks the other person to take nothing on your say-so. It builds only on what critical scholars grant, including atheists. Then it asks one question. What explains all of it?

Jesus of Nazareth was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Bart Ehrman calls that one of the most secure facts in ancient history. Tacitus and Josephus both mention it. Second, soon after, his followers had experiences they were sure were appearances of him alive. Gerd Lüdemann was an atheist New Testament scholar. He wrote that it is "historically certain that Peter and the disciples had experiences after Jesus's death in which Jesus appeared to them as the risen Christ."

plain.t: The third fact, and the honest caveat
plain.d: The preaching began in Jerusalem almost at once. Paul, who had been hunting the movement down, changed sides. So did James, the skeptical brother of Jesus. The empty tomb is more disputed, and say so. Gary Habermas's much-quoted "about 75%" figure counts published articles, not scholars polled. Ehrman doubts even the burial by Joseph of Arimathea. The Gospels do have women find the tomb, whose word carried little legal weight, and that still counts in its favour.

Ehrman replies that every granted fact has a natural cause. Visions of the recently dead are well documented in grief research. A few sincere visions among shattered followers, read through Jewish hopes about the end, then retold for decades, gives you all we have. Mark, our first Gospel, has no appearance stories. Crucified men were often left unburied. The women point leans on the criterion of embarrassment, which Rafael Rodríguez and the memory-studies school now treat as shaky. Sincere change of life shows conviction, not its cause. The Millerites and the followers of Sabbatai Zevi were transformed too.

The facts are granted by the field's leading skeptics, in print. The real fight is the step from those facts to a risen Jesus. Say that out loud. You will be the most honest Christian that person has met. And never quote the 75% figure without its caveat.
"Forget my Bible for a minute. Here are five things your side already grants. What explains them?"

title: The 1 Corinthians 15 creed: resurrection belief within about five years, not legendary centuries
claim: In 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, written around AD 54-55, Paul quotes a formula he says he 'received' and 'delivered'. That is the technical rabbinic vocabulary for handing on a tradition. Its non-Pauline Semitic features — 'the Twelve', 'according to the Scriptures', parallel clauses — mark it as older than Paul. He most plausibly received it in Damascus after his conversion, around AD 33-36, or at his Jerusalem visit with Peter and James about three years later (Galatians 1:18). This is not an apologetic claim. It is the critical consensus. The atheist Gerd Lüdemann dates the creed's elements within two to three years of the crucifixion, and James D. G. Dunn says the tradition was 'formulated within months'. The consequence matters. 'Died, buried, raised, appeared to Peter, the Twelve, five hundred, James, all the apostles' was fixed public tradition while hundreds of eyewitnesses, hostile and friendly, were still alive. Legend needs generations and distance — compare the Alexander romances, which appear centuries after Alexander. The resurrection proclamation had neither. Conspiracy theories fare no better, since the creed predates any institutional church with anything to gain.

sources.name: 1 Corinthians 15 (text)
Wikipedia, '1 Corinthians 15' (creed scholarship survey)
James D. G. Dunn, Jesus Remembered
Gary Habermas on the creed's dating

response: The strongest skeptical use of the creed accepts its date and turns it. Early attestation of belief is not early attestation of events. The verb Paul uses for 'appeared' (ōphthē) is the same one he uses for his own Damascus experience, which Acts describes as light and a voice rather than a touchable body. Paul puts his own vision in the same list as Peter's, which suggests all the appearances may have been visionary. The creed contains no empty tomb. And apocalyptic movements demonstrably generate firm supernatural convictions within weeks rather than generations. The Millerites reinterpreted the Great Disappointment within days. Rapid, sincere and early — and still explicable as visionary experience crystallising into a formula.
rationale: Admitted tier. The early dating is conceded right across the spectrum, from Habermas to Lüdemann, and it permanently retires the claim that the resurrection is a legend which grew over centuries. That claim is still common at the popular level, and correcting it gently is a service. Present the creed as demolishing the legend and conspiracy timelines. Then honestly note the skeptic's fallback — early belief is not true belief — and pivot to the real question, which is what best explains the origin of the belief.

plain.d: 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 was written about AD 54-55. In it Paul quotes something older than his letter. He says he "received" it and "delivered" it. Those are the standard rabbinic words for handing on a tradition. The wording is not his usual style. It has Hebrew-shaped features: "the Twelve," "according to the Scriptures," matched clauses.

Paul most likely received it in Damascus after he changed sides, around AD 33-36. Or in Jerusalem with Peter and James about three years later (Galatians 1:18). This is not an apologist's date. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist, puts the parts of the creed within two to three years of the crucifixion. James D. G. Dunn says the tradition was "formulated within months."

So the list was fixed public teaching while witnesses were still alive, friendly and hostile. Died, buried, raised, appeared to Peter, the Twelve, five hundred, James, all the apostles. Legends need distance and generations. The tall tales about Alexander took centuries. This had neither. And there was no church yet with anything to gain.

The best skeptics accept the date and turn it round. Early belief is not early proof. Paul's word for "appeared" is the same one he uses for his own Damascus experience, which Acts describes as light and a voice, not a body you could touch. He lists his own experience alongside Peter's. Perhaps they were all visions. The creed says nothing about an empty tomb. And groups do produce firm supernatural convictions fast. The Millerites reworked their failed prediction within days.

Granted on all sides, from Gary Habermas to Lüdemann. It retires one common claim for good. The resurrection is not a legend that grew over centuries. Then give the fallback honestly. Early belief is not true belief. Move the talk to what caused the belief.
"This creed is older than the letter it sits in. Whatever started it, it started within a few years."

title: Hallucination theories, steelmanned — and where they strain
claim: Take the best naturalistic explanation seriously, because skeptics do. Bereavement 'presence' experiences are common, with roughly half of surviving spouses reporting a sense of the dead. Grief visions for Peter, guilt-resolution for Paul, and cognitive-dissonance reduction in the manner of Festinger for the movement as a whole: that is the serious skeptical package, and it deserves respect. Now its strains. Grief visions are private, occasional, and recognised by the person as visions. They do not typically produce the claim that a man is bodily risen now. In Judaism, resurrection was a corporate, end-of-history event, not something that happened to one man mid-history — the point N. T. Wright presses. Group experiences do not fit hallucination's clinical profile, which is private by nature, and the sources report the Twelve and 'more than five hundred at once', whom Paul says could still be questioned. Paul was not grieving; he was persecuting. James was an unbelieving brother (Mark 3:21; John 7:5) who became leader of the Jerusalem church and died for it, as Josephus records. A theory has to cover all of it: skeptic, enemy, groups, and an empty tomb that no one refuted by producing a body.

sources.name: N. T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God (Jewish resurrection expectation)
Michael Licona, The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach
Josephus, Antiquities 20 (death of James)
Paulogia (the leading popular-level naturalistic case)

response: The disciplined skeptical version — Ehrman, Richard Carrier, and Paulogia's 'minimal witnesses' model — needs far less than apologists attack. Perhaps only Peter and Paul had visionary experiences. The only appearance we have any first-person account of is Paul's, and it reads as a vision. The group appearances exist for us solely as one-line creed items, or as Gospel narratives written decades later by non-eyewitnesses. The five hundred are uncorroborated anywhere else. James's conversion by an appearance is an inference, since no text narrates it. Shared religious ecstasy in expectant communities is well documented, from the Toronto Blessing to Marian apparitions, and movements routinely survive disconfirmation with strengthened faith. The theory does not need mass hallucinations. It needs one or two visions plus forty years of telling.
rationale: Contested, graded honestly, because the sophisticated skeptical model — a few visions plus decades of development — is much harder to dispatch than the strawman about five hundred people sharing one hallucination. Steelman it first, always. The Christian case is strongest on the conjunction: Paul the enemy, James the brother, the empty tomb, and an immediate bodily resurrection claim in a Jewish context that had no category for it. Michael Licona's historiographical work presses that conjunction. Argue the conjunction, never a single thread.

plain.d: Grief visions are real and common. About half of surviving spouses report sensing the dead. So the skeptical package deserves respect. A grief vision for Peter. Guilt resolving itself for Paul. And for the group, what Festinger called cognitive dissonance, where a belief hardens after it is threatened.

Grief visions are private, occasional, and known by the person to be visions. They do not usually produce the claim that a man is bodily alive now. N. T. Wright makes the point well. In Judaism, resurrection was an event at the end of history, for everyone at once. Not something that happened to one man in the middle of it.

Group experiences: the Twelve, and "more than five hundred at once," whom Paul says could still be asked. Hallucinations are private by clinical nature. Paul was not grieving. He was hunting Christians down (Acts 9:1-9). James did not believe in his brother (Mark 3:21; John 7:5), then led the Jerusalem church and died for it, which Josephus records. And nobody produced a body.

The disciplined version needs far less than Christians attack. Ehrman, Richard Carrier and the popular case-maker Paulogia use a minimal-witnesses model. Perhaps only Peter and Paul had visions. The only first-person account we have is Paul's, and it reads like one. The group appearances reach us as a single creed line, or as Gospels written decades later by non-witnesses. The five hundred are backed up nowhere else. No text actually narrates James seeing anything. And shared religious ecstasy in expectant groups is well documented, from the Toronto Blessing to Marian apparitions.

Contested, honestly. The clever version is much harder to beat than the strawman about five hundred people sharing one hallucination. So argue the whole set at once. The enemy, the brother, the tomb, and a bodily claim that Judaism had no slot for. Michael Licona's book works that ground. Never argue a single thread.
"Grief visions are real, I grant that. But Paul wasn't grieving. He was on the other side."

title: The New Testament text: the best-attested document of antiquity — with the variant count told honestly
claim: The New Testament survives in about 5,800 Greek manuscripts, plus tens of thousands more in early versions, with fragments such as P52 within decades of composition. Compare Tacitus's Annals: about 20 substantial manuscripts, copied a millennium after he wrote. Now the honest version of the variant question. Yes, there are more than 400,000 variants — more variants than there are words in the New Testament, as Ehrman says on tour. But that number scales with manuscript abundance. More copies means more variants, which means more data, and the vast majority are spelling, word order and obvious slips. The two large disputed passages, Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11, are bracketed with notes in every modern Bible. That is transparency, not cover-up. And here is Ehrman himself, in the paperback appendix of Misquoting Jesus: 'The position I argue for in Misquoting Jesus does not actually stand at odds with Prof. Metzger's position that the essential Christian beliefs are not affected by textual variants in the manuscript tradition of the New Testament.' Quote that fairly. It is his own words, in his own book.

sources.name: Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts (Daniel Wallace)
Bart Ehrman, Misquoting Jesus, 2007 paperback appendix Q&A
Wikipedia, 'Textual variants in the New Testament'
Peter J. Williams, Can We Trust the Gospels? (Crossway)

response: Ehrman's serious point survives his concession. Abundant late manuscripts do not fix the earliest period. Our manuscript flood begins in the third century. The first 150 years or so are nearly a black box, and that is precisely when copying was done by amateurs, the text was most fluid, and the most consequential changes could occur. Some variants do matter theologically: the angry versus the compassionate Jesus of Mark 1:41, Luke's bloody sweat, the doxology endings. And 'no cardinal doctrine affected' partly reflects the fact that doctrines were later formulated from the surviving text. Deeper still, 'the original text' is itself a fuzzy target if compositions circulated in editions. We have excellent access to the second-century text. The autographs remain an inference.
rationale: Admitted. The attestation superiority is a plain bibliographic fact, and the point that no essential doctrine hangs on a variant is conceded by the field's most famous skeptic in print. Never quote raw manuscript counts without the honest context — most are medieval, and variants scale with copies. A skeptic who knows the field will spring that trap otherwise. Concede the early-period gap. The claim that survives is 'we know what the New Testament authors wrote to within trivial margins', not 'we have photocopies of the autographs'.

plain.d: The New Testament survives in about 5,800 Greek manuscripts. Add tens of thousands more in early translations. One scrap, P52, is within decades of when John was written. Compare the Annals of Tacitus: about 20 substantial copies, made a thousand years after he wrote.

There are more than 400,000 differences between the copies. That is more variants than there are words in the New Testament, as Bart Ehrman says on tour. Here is why the number is so big. More copies means more countable differences. Nearly all are spelling, word order and obvious slips. Two long passages are genuinely disputed: Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11. Every modern Bible brackets them with a note. That is transparency, not a cover-up.

In the paperback appendix of Misquoting Jesus, Ehrman wrote that his position "does not actually stand at odds with Prof. Metzger's position that the essential Christian beliefs are not affected by textual variants in the manuscript tradition of the New Testament." Quote it fairly. It is his own book.

His serious point survives that concession. Plentiful late copies do not fix the earliest years. The flood of manuscripts begins in the third century. The first 150 years are nearly a blank, and that is when amateurs copied and the text moved most. Some variants do carry weight. Mark 1:41 has an angry or a compassionate Jesus. Luke has the bloody sweat. The endings differ. And "no doctrine affected" partly reflects that doctrines were framed later, from the text that survived. Deeper still, "the original" is fuzzy if a book circulated in editions.

Granted, and by the field's most famous skeptic in print. But never quote raw counts without the context. Most of those copies are medieval, and variants scale with copies. Someone who knows the field will spring that trap. Concede the early gap. What stands is this. We know what the authors wrote, to within trivial margins. Not that we hold photocopies.
"Most of those 400,000 differences are spelling. I'll show you the two that actually matter."

title: The Dead Sea Scrolls: a thousand-year transmission test, passed
claim: Before 1947, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts came from around AD 1000, in the Masoretic tradition. That left skeptics free to argue that a thousand years of copying had rewritten the text. Then the Qumran caves gave up biblical manuscripts a thousand years older. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) contains the entire book. Radiocarbon and handwriting date it to roughly 125 BC. Set against the Masoretic text of a thousand years later, it is much the same. Nearly all the differences are spelling habits and slips. Only a handful of readings affect meaning, and none affect doctrine. This is a direct measurement of scribal care across ten centuries — the exact test skeptics said the text would fail. Honesty requires the caveat. Qumran also shows real variety in some books. Jeremiah exists in a short and a long edition, and Samuel differs. So the right claim is that copying was astonishingly careful, and that where it was not, we can see it. Not that it was letter-perfect.

Wikipedia, 'Isaiah Scroll' (dating and MT comparison)
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (the standard reference)
Wikipedia, 'Dead Sea Scrolls'

response: The careful skeptical framing is this. The scrolls prove faithful copying from about 125 BC onward. They say nothing about the centuries between the writing of a book and Qumran. That is where critical scholars place the heavy editing. Isaiah itself is widely held to gather material from the eighth through the sixth centuries BC, and the scrolls cannot settle that. The variety at Qumran also cuts against a simple one-text story, since the community shelved rival editions of Jeremiah and Samuel side by side. That suggests the settled text was still in motion. And copying a text well has nothing to do with whether the text is true. A perfectly copied oracle is still just an oracle.
rationale: Admitted. The date of 1QIsaa and its closeness to the Masoretic text are uncontested facts. The Israel Museum published them, and every textual critic accepts them, skeptics included. Emanuel Tov's standard handbook sets out both halves. Claim exactly what it proves. A thousand years of proven care in copying, plus hard physical proof that Isaiah 53 is older than Jesus, which matters for the prophecy entries. Raise the Jeremiah and Samuel caveat yourself, before the skeptic does.

title: How the canon actually formed — and why the Da Vinci Code version is folklore
claim: The pop-culture story is that Constantine and the Council of Nicaea in 325 picked the Gospels and suppressed the rest. It is false, and not by apologetic special pleading — Bart Ehrman wrote a book correcting it. Nicaea debated Arianism, and no canon list was on its agenda. The real history is earlier and more organic. Paul's letters circulated as a collection by the early second century, and P46, from about AD 200, is a bound Pauline codex; 2 Peter 3:16 already calls them 'scriptures'. Irenaeus, around 180, treats the fourfold Gospel as settled and obvious. The Muratorian fragment, dated about 170-200 on the majority view, lists most of the New Testament. The criteria were public: apostolic connection, universal usage, and coherence with the received faith. The so-called Gnostic gospels are second-century-and-later compositions that no church used broadly, and that nobody dates within eyewitness range. The edges genuinely wobbled until the fourth century — Hebrews, Revelation and 2-3 John, with Hermas and Barnabas read in some churches — and honesty says so. But the core was fixed by usage, not by imperial vote, within living memory of the apostolic generation.

sources.name: Bart Ehrman, Truth and Fiction in The Da Vinci Code
Wikipedia, 'Development of the New Testament canon'
Wikipedia, 'Muratorian fragment'
Michael Kruger, Canon Fodder

response: The scholarly skeptical version drops Dan Brown and picks up Walter Bauer. Earliest Christianity was wildly diverse — Marcionites, Ebionites, Valentinians — and 'orthodoxy' is simply the name of the faction that won and then wrote the history, canonising its own texts and calling the criteria objective. Those criteria were arguably circular, since 'apostolic' and 'orthodox' were judged by the very proto-orthodox standard being defended. Some scholars hold that the Gospel of Thomas preserves independent early Jesus tradition. And the wobbling edges undermine the tidy story. Churches disagreed about Revelation and Hebrews for two centuries. If canonicity were evident, why the centuries of dispute?
rationale: Admitted for the load-bearing claim. No serious scholar, however skeptical, defends the Nicaea-canon myth, and Ehrman debunks it in print, which makes him the perfect citation. The Bauer-thesis counter is real but weaker than its reputation, since the fourfold Gospel's early and geographically wide dominance is hard for it to explain. Correcting the Da Vinci folklore gently, with Ehrman as your source, is a credibility-building move with skeptics who absorbed it from the culture. Concede the wobbly edges cheerfully; Michael Kruger's work covers them.

plain.t: The story most people have heard
plain.d: Constantine and the Council of Nicaea in 325 picked the four Gospels and buried the rest. That is false. And you do not have to take a Christian's word for it. Bart Ehrman wrote a book correcting it. Nicaea argued about Arianism. No list of books was on its agenda.

Paul's letters were moving as a set by the early second century. P46, from about AD 200, is a bound book of them. 2 Peter 3:16 already calls them "scriptures." Around 180, Irenaeus treats the four Gospels as settled and obvious. The Muratorian fragment, dated about 170-200 by most, lists most of the New Testament. The tests were public. Apostolic link, wide use, and fit with the faith already received.

plain.t: The other gospels, and the wobbly edges
plain.d: The Gnostic gospels are second-century or later. No church used them widely. Nobody dates them within witness range. But the edges did wobble, and say so. Hebrews, Revelation and 2-3 John were argued over into the fourth century. Hermas and Barnabas were read in some churches. A list from AD 367 finally matches the New Testament you own.

Serious skeptics drop Dan Brown and pick up Walter Bauer. Earliest Christianity was wildly varied, with Marcionites, Ebionites and Valentinians. "Orthodoxy" is just the name of the side that won and then wrote the history. The tests look circular too. Apostolic and orthodox were judged by the very standard being defended. Some scholars think the Gospel of Thomas keeps early sayings of its own. And if the right books were obvious, why two centuries of argument about Revelation?

Granted on the load-bearing part. No serious scholar defends the Nicaea story, and Ehrman debunks it in print. That makes him the perfect person to cite. The Bauer thesis is real but weaker than its reputation. The four Gospels were dominant early and over a wide area. Concede the wobbly edges cheerfully. Michael Kruger is worth reading on the rest.
"The Nicaea story isn't true, and my source for that is Bart Ehrman, not a pastor."

title: The spade and the kings: Tel Dan, Hezekiah's tunnel, Sennacherib, Cyrus
claim: Within living scholarly memory it was respectable to call King David a legend, like Arthur. Then in 1993 the Tel Dan stele surfaced. It is a victory inscription in Aramaic from the ninth century BC, and it bears 'bytdwd', the House of David. That is a royal line named within about 140 years of David's life. The minimalist reading, 'temple of Dod', has been all but abandoned. Hezekiah's tunnel runs under Jerusalem, with the Siloam inscription cut by the workmen. It matches the one-line note about the same works in 2 Kings 20:20. Sennacherib's own prism boasts of shutting Hezekiah up 'like a caged bird' in Jerusalem in 701 BC. It does not claim the city fell, which matches the account in 2 Kings 19 of a siege that ended for no stated reason. The Cyrus Cylinder sets out the Persian policy of sending exiled peoples home and rebuilding their shrines. That is the exact policy Ezra 1 assumes. The pattern holds. Where the Bible can be tested against dirt and stone, it keeps turning out to be about real kings, real wars and real waterworks.

sources.name: Wikipedia, 'Tel Dan stele'
Wikipedia, 'Siloam inscription' / Hezekiah's tunnel
Wikipedia, 'Sennacherib's Annals' (Taylor Prism)
British Museum / Wikipedia, 'Cyrus Cylinder'
Biblical Archaeology Society

response: Israel Finkelstein and the minimalist-leaning mainstream reply that a king who existed is not a thing God did. Tel Dan proves a line of David, not a united kingdom on the scale the Bible describes. Archaeology still contests that, through the low chronology and the thin tenth-century remains in Jerusalem. Sennacherib's withdrawal has natural causes. His own prism says Hezekiah paid heavily, and disease or Egyptian pressure are on the table too. The Cyrus Cylinder describes broad Persian policy, not Israel in particular. And the same spade creates problems that entries like this one leave out. Jericho was a ruin centuries before any likely Joshua, and the exodus has left no trace in Sinai. Archaeology confirms the setting. It stays carefully neutral about the miracles.
rationale: Admitted for the finds themselves. Tel Dan, the tunnel, the prism and the cylinder are undisputed facts on display in museums, and the House of David reading is now agreed on all sides. Claim the right thing. The Bible is history-shaped writing about real people and events, proved right again and again against confident doubt. Then grant at once that stones confirm kings, not theology. Do not hide the Jericho problem. A skeptic who knows it will respect you for raising it first.

title: Pilate's stone, Caiaphas's bones, and John's pools: the New Testament's world checks out
claim: In 1961 a limestone block at Caesarea Maritima gave us Pontius Pilate's name in stone, with the title 'prefect of Judea' — the technically correct title for his period, which even Tacitus got wrong by writing 'procurator'. In 1990 an ornate ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas' was found in Jerusalem, very likely the high priest of the passion narratives. John's Gospel was long accused of geographic fantasy. It describes a Pool of Bethesda with five colonnades, an odd architectural detail. Excavation found a double pool with four surrounding porticoes and one across the middle: five. The Pool of Siloam of John 9 was uncovered in 2004. Nazareth's existence, denied by internet mythicism in the person of René Salm, is settled: a first-century house published by the Israel Antiquities Authority in 2009, the Nazareth Village Farm remains, and the Caesarea inscription listing the town among the priestly courses. The claim is so weak that atheist historians such as Tim O'Neill debunk it to keep their own side honest. The Gospels' incidental details keep landing in the right century, the right city, and the right posthole.

Wikipedia, 'Caiaphas ossuary'
Wikipedia, 'Pool of Bethesda'
Tim O'Neill, History for Atheists (atheist debunking of Nazareth mythicism)
Peter J. Williams, Can We Trust the Gospels? (onomastics and local detail)

response: Accurate scenery is not evidence of accurate miracles. Gone with the Wind gets Atlanta right. The serious version runs like this: John's topographic accuracy shows his tradition includes reliable pre-70 memory of Jerusalem, which critical scholars happily grant while still dating the Gospel to about 90-110 and denying eyewitness authorship. Local colour survives in communities, not just in eyewitnesses. The Caiaphas ossuary identification, while plausible, is debated, since the inscription's spelling and the tomb's modesty give some scholars pause. Pilate and Caiaphas were famous officials, and a story set in Judea could hardly avoid them. Corroborating the cast list is the floor of historical reliability, not the ceiling. No pool ever excavated a healing.
rationale: Admitted. Every find listed is real, published and uncontested in its essentials, and the Nazareth-mythicism debunk comes best from atheist historians — cite O'Neill, not an apologist, for maximum effect. Frame the whole set as cumulative erosion of the 'Gospels as late fantasy' picture. Texts wrong about everything do not keep being right about porticoes and prefects' titles. Concede freely that stones corroborate settings, not signs. Peter J. Williams collects more of this kind of detail.

plain.d: In 1961 a block of stone at Caesarea Maritima turned up with Pontius Pilate's name on it. It gives his title as prefect of Judea. That is the right one for his years. John's Gospel was long accused of inventing its geography. It describes a Pool of Bethesda with five colonnades, which is an odd number for a building. Excavation found a double pool. Four porticoes around it, and one across the middle. Five. The Pool of Siloam of John 9 was uncovered in 2004, during a sewer repair.

René Salm and other online mythicists claim Nazareth did not exist in the first century. It is settled. A house from that century was dug up and published in 2009 by the Israel Antiquities Authority. There are the Nazareth Village Farm remains. And a stone list from Caesarea names the town among the priestly courses. The claim is so weak that Tim O'Neill, an atheist, debunks it to keep his own side honest.

Concede freely that stones confirm settings, not signs. Peter J. Williams collects more of this.
"John said the pool had five colonnades. People called that a mistake for centuries. Then they dug it up."

title: The census of Quirinius: a real difficulty, handled the honest way
claim: This entry models something the site believes: honest apologetics concedes real problems. Luke 2:2 dates Jesus's birth to a census 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria'. Josephus places Quirinius's census in AD 6, but Matthew and Luke both put the birth under Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC. That is a collision of roughly ten years, and it is the single strongest 'Luke erred' datum skeptics possess. The proposed harmonisations exist. Luke 2:2 can be translated 'before the census under Quirinius', which most Greek scholars judge grammatically strained. An earlier Quirinius command in Syria has been proposed, but the Lapis Tiburtinus inscription is missing the crucial name. Recurring registration cycles have been proposed too. None of these commands assent, and Raymond Brown — a believing Catholic scholar and the standard authority on the infancy narratives — concluded that Luke probably got the mechanism wrong. What survives is Luke's demonstrated precision elsewhere: Acts's titles, routes and officials check out in detail, and Hemer catalogued scores of confirmed specifics. And no Christian doctrine rests on census administration. Concede the problem, and keep the perspective.

sources.name: Wikipedia, 'Census of Quirinius' (full problem and proposed solutions)
Raymond Brown, The Birth of the Messiah
Josephus, Antiquities 18 (the AD 6 census)
Wikipedia, 'Historical reliability of the Acts of the Apostles' (Hemer's data)

response: The skeptic's point is the difficulty itself, and it extends further. Luke's census mechanics are implausible on their own terms. Rome taxed people where they lived and owned property, and no empire-wide decree sent men to ancestral towns a millennium back. The simplest explanation is that Luke, writing decades later, constructed a narrative device to move a Galilean family to Bethlehem, where messianic prophecy in Micah 5:2 required the birth. Matthew moves the family by a different and incompatible device, since in his account they seem to live in Bethlehem and relocate to Nazareth. Two independent authors solving the same theological problem with contradictory mechanisms suggests that the Bethlehem birth itself may be theology rather than memory.
rationale: Contested — and this entry's chief purpose is pedagogical, showing a Christian audience how to concede a genuine difficulty without the sky falling. Never deploy the strained harmonisations as if they were solid. Say instead: this is the best single card in the skeptic's deck on Luke, the harmonisations are possible but unproven, and Christianity does not stand or fall on it. A skeptic who hears a Christian say that will listen to the resurrection case with different ears. Evidential weight for the positive case is low. This is defence, done honestly.

title: Tyre and Babylon: impressive fulfillments, real complications — don't overclaim
claim: Here is the honest version. Ezekiel 26, from the early sixth century BC, pronounced doom on the island city of Tyre: many nations against it, walls broken, rubble scraped into the sea, a bare rock for spreading nets. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years and took the mainland city, but not the island or its wealth. And here is the remarkable part. Ezekiel 29:17-20 records the shortfall, saying that Nebuchadnezzar 'got no wages' from Tyre, and redirecting him to Egypt. The text preserves its own unfulfilled expectation, which is powerful evidence that these oracles were not doctored after the fact. Two and a half centuries later, Alexander built his famous causeway out of the mainland ruins — literally scraping Tyre into the sea — and took the island. Babylon, the greatest city on earth when Isaiah and Jeremiah pronounced its perpetual desolation, declined over centuries into exactly that. What to drop: 'Tyre was never rebuilt', since modern Tyre has about 200,000 people, and 'fulfilled to the letter, overnight'. What stands: named cities at their height, assigned improbable fates, that history then delivered — gradually, partially, and with the text honest about the gaps.

response: The skeptical reading is this. Ezekiel 26 plainly expected Nebuchadnezzar to do all of it, and the 'many nations' reading that spreads fulfilment across 250 years to Alexander is a rescue device. Ezekiel 29's own admission proves the original prediction failed as issued. Ancient doom oracles against rival cities were a genre, and given enough centuries every great ancient city was sacked and most declined. Babylon's fate is base-rate history, not prescience — its desolation took eight hundred years, was never total, and Saddam rebuilt sections of it. Predictions that are vague on timing and agent, scored generously across millennia, cannot be distinguished from a prophet playing the odds against cities everyone already wanted dead.
rationale: Contested — grade it exactly there, and lead with Ezekiel 29's self-correction, which converts an apparent liability into the strongest point available. Texts fabricated after the fact do not record their own misses. Never say 'never rebuilt', and never compress the timeline. If you overclaim Tyre, the skeptic who checks will discount everything else you said. This entry earns its keep as a model of restrained prophecy apologetics.

title: Daniel's date: the late-date case steelmanned, and what survives either way
claim: Be upfront: the critical consensus dates Daniel's final form to the 160s BC, and the case is serious. Daniel 11 tracks Ptolemaic-Seleucid history with uncanny precision up to Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Then verses 40-45 predict Antiochus's end in ways that do not match how he actually died in 163 BC. That is the classic signature, first noted by the pagan critic Porphyry, of 'prophecy' written during the events and failing only where it ventures past its author's present. Add the Greek loanwords, Daniel's placement outside the Prophets in the Hebrew canon, and Sirach's silence around 180 BC. The traditional-date minority answers back. K. A. Kitchen argues the Aramaic is Imperial Aramaic of an earlier profile. Daniel knows that Belshazzar was coregent under the absent Nabonidus, a detail lost to later Greek historians and recovered only from cuneiform, which is hard for a Maccabean author to know. And Qumran's multiple Daniel manuscripts from about 125 BC, together with the book's rapid canonical prestige, are tight for a fresh pseudepigraphon. Note also what survives even on the late date. Daniel 7's 'son of man' and Daniel 9's timeline predate Jesus and shaped the messianic expectation he stepped into.

response: John J. Collins, who wrote the standard critical commentary, makes the consensus case. Chapter 11's accuracy followed by failure at verse 40 is as close to a dating fingerprint as ancient literature provides. The genre — apocalyptic pseudepigraphy, prophecy after the event — was common, and its original audiences likely understood the convention. The Belshazzar coregency could plausibly survive in Babylonian-Jewish memory streams, and the Prayer of Nabonidus at Qumran shows such traditions circulating. The linguistic arguments cut both ways, and few Aramaicists find them decisive. Sixty years from composition around 165 BC to our earliest copies around 125 BC is unusually tight, but pseudepigrapha achieved acceptance quickly in that era, as 1 Enoch did. On scholarly headcount this is not close. The late date holds the field.
rationale: Contested — and the rationale must be candid that the traditional early date is the minority position. So do not lead with Daniel in a conversation with an informed skeptic. You will spend the whole evening on Aramaic. The durable point is the fallback. Even granting 165 BC, the son-of-man figure and the messianic timetable are pre-Christian, which feeds the logic of the Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 entry. Deploy that, not the dating fight.

Daniel 11 tracks the wars of the Greek successor kingdoms with uncanny precision, right up to Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Then verses 40-45 predict his end, and it does not match how he actually died in 163 BC. The pagan critic Porphyry noticed that first. It is the classic signature of prophecy written during the events, failing only where it goes past its author's own day. Add Greek loanwords, Daniel's place outside the Prophets in the Hebrew canon, and Sirach's silence about him around 180 BC.

K. A. Kitchen argues that Daniel's Aramaic fits an earlier Imperial profile. Daniel also knows that Belshazzar ruled as coregent while Nabonidus was away. Later Greek historians lost that detail, and it was recovered only from cuneiform. That is hard for a writer in the 160s to know. Qumran holds several Daniel manuscripts from about 125 BC. Sixty years from writing to copies, plus fast standing as scripture, is tight for a fresh forgery.

John J. Collins wrote the standard critical commentary. Chapter 11's accuracy, then failure at verse 40, is as close to a dating fingerprint as ancient writing offers. The genre, apocalyptic work under a borrowed name, was common, and the first readers likely knew the convention. The Belshazzar detail could survive in Babylonian-Jewish memory. The Prayer of Nabonidus at Qumran shows such traditions circulating. Few Aramaic specialists find the language argument decisive. And 1 Enoch won acceptance fast too. On headcount, this is not close.

Contested, and be candid. The early date is the minority position. So do not lead with Daniel against an informed skeptic. You will spend the whole evening on Aramaic. The durable point is the fallback. Even at 165 BC, Daniel 7's "son of man" and Daniel 9's timetable are older than Jesus. They shaped the hope he walked into.
"Grant the late date. Daniel's son of man is still older than Jesus, and that's the part I care about."

title: Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22: the Dead Sea Scrolls prove the texts came first
claim: Strip this argument to the part that is physically certain. The Great Isaiah Scroll contains all of Isaiah 53 — the servant despised, pierced for others' transgressions, silent before his shearers, numbered with transgressors, buried with the rich, seeing light after death. It sits in the Israel Museum and dates to roughly 125 BC, more than a century before the crucifixion. Psalm 22 — the mockery, 'why have you forsaken me', the divided garments, the casting of lots, the encircled hands and feet — was translated into Greek generations before Jesus. Whatever one concludes about these texts, one hypothesis is dead on arrival: that Christians wrote or edited them after the fact to fit Jesus. The correspondence between Israel's most famous suffering-figure texts and the manner of Jesus's death is either coincidence, or literary construction by the evangelists, or design. But the texts' priority is not a faith claim. It is carbon-dated parchment. This is the strongest form of the prophecy argument. Begin from what is physically beyond dispute, and then argue about interpretation.

sources.name: Great Isaiah Scroll, Israel Museum (view Isaiah 53 online)
Wikipedia, 'Isaiah 53' (Jewish and Christian interpretation history)
Psalm 22 (text)
Wikipedia, 'Psalm 22' (incl. the 22:16 textual question)

response: The mainstream Jewish and critical reading is that Isaiah's servant is Israel. The text says so repeatedly in the surrounding chapters — 'you are my servant, Israel' at Isaiah 41:8, 44:1 and 49:3 — suffering in exile and vindicated in the return. On that reading, chapter 53 is not a messianic prediction in context. Psalm 22 is an individual lament, a genre piece rather than a prophecy. And the match has a simpler explanation. The passion narratives were composed using these texts. The evangelists, writing decades later, narrated the crucifixion in the language of Psalm 22, and Mark hands you the psalm's first line from the cross. So of course the events fit the texts: the texts shaped the telling. Psalm 22:16's 'pierced' also rests on a genuine textual crux, the Masoretic 'like a lion' against the ka'aru reading, and is too disputed to bear weight.
rationale: Admitted — strictly for the pre-dating, which is the entry's actual claim, and which is conceded by everyone with a radiocarbon lab. The messianic interpretation is genuinely contested, and the two layers must be kept apart. This is the answer to 'the prophecies were written in after the fact', full stop. Against the servant-as-Israel reading, note honestly that the servant in chapter 53 suffers vicariously for 'my people', and that some pre-Christian Jewish tradition read the passage messianically. Then let the texts do their own work. Do not hang anything on Psalm 22:16's disputed word.

title: The problem of evil: the skeptic's best argument, answered within its limits
claim: Take it at full strength, because it deserves it. William Rowe's fawn: a deer burns slowly to death in a forest fire that no human ever knows about. What greater good does that serve? Paul Draper adds that the actual distribution of pain and pleasure looks exactly like what biological indifference predicts, and not like what a loving Father predicts. This is the skeptic's best card, and many deconverts hold it not as philosophy but as autopsy — a child's grave, an unanswered prayer. The Christian responses, honestly labelled, run as follows. The logical problem is widely regarded as answered, and even J. L. Mackie conceded that Plantinga's free-will defence shows 'the problem of evil does not, after all, show that the central doctrines of theism are logically inconsistent'. The evidential problem remains. Free will, soul-making in John Hick's sense, and skeptical theism — the view that we are poorly positioned to certify any suffering as pointless — each carry real weight and real costs. Scripture's own answer to Job is not a theodicy but a presence. And Christianity's distinctive is a God with wounds: the cross puts God inside the problem rather than above it.

sources.name: SEP, 'The Problem of Evil' (Tooley)
J. L. Mackie, The Miracle of Theism (the concession on the logical problem)
Alvin Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil
Paul Draper's evidential argument (overview)
C. S. Lewis, A Grief Observed (the pastoral register)

response: Rowe and Draper, pressed properly, answer back. Skeptical theism saves God at the price of skepticism about everything. If we cannot judge the fawn's suffering pointless, then we also cannot judge anything God-commanded as good, and moral knowledge collapses. Free will is irrelevant to earthquakes, parasites, and the 500 million years of animal suffering that preceded any human choice. Soul-making fails for suffering that destroys souls rather than building them — childhood dementia, and the fawn, which has no soul to make. Draper's comparative point stands un-answered rather than answered: on the hypothesis of indifference, the biological role of pain is expected, while on theism it requires auxiliary hypotheses stacked ad hoc. The cross may console. It does not explain.
rationale: Contested — anyone who grades this 'answered' has not felt it. The honest position is that the logical problem is resolved, with Mackie's concession in print, while the evidential problem is a genuine open wound. Christianity's resources — free will, soul-making, eschatology, the cross — reduce its force but do not eliminate it. There is a pastoral rule here, and it is non-negotiable. With a suffering person, arguments are the wrong tool, and Job's friends were at their best in the seven silent days. This entry is for the whiteboard, never the hospital room.

title: Divine hiddenness: Schellenberg's argument and the shape of a God who wants love, not compliance
claim: J. L. Schellenberg's argument, stated fairly, runs like this. A perfectly loving God would ensure that a conscious relationship is available to every creature open to one. Yet 'nonresistant nonbelief' exists — people who sought God sincerely, sometimes through years of anguished prayer, and found silence. Many deconverts are exhibit A, and the first Christian response must be to believe them. Their seeking was real, and 'you secretly resisted' is both unkind and unfounded. The substantive responses are these. Paul Moser argues that God's aim is filial knowledge — love that transforms — rather than spectator certainty, and that evidence sufficient to compel assent without surrender might produce precisely the wrong relationship. Pascal saw the same asymmetry: 'enough light for those who desire to see, enough obscurity for those of a contrary disposition'. Scripture itself testifies to the experience — 'Truly, you are a God who hides himself' (Isaiah 45:15) — and a third of the Psalms are lament at the silence. The Christian claim was never that God is obvious. It is that he is findable, sought with the whole heart (Jeremiah 29:13), and known finally in a person rather than a proof.

sources.name: SEP, 'Divine Hiddenness' (Schellenberg's own entry)
J. L. Schellenberg, Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason
Paul Moser, The Elusive God (CUP)
Blaise Pascal, Pensées (light/obscurity fragments)

response: Schellenberg's rejoinders are strong. A relationship requires believing that the other party exists, and a loving parent does not hide so thoroughly that the child doubts she has a parent. Whatever goods obscurity secures, an omnipotent God could secure them alongside basic awareness of his existence. The 'wrong kind of belief' worry conflates knowing that God exists with surrendering to him. The demons of James 2:19 manage the first without the second, which proves the two come apart, so clarity coerces nothing. And Stephen Maitzen's demographic point bites: nonbelief clusters by geography and upbringing, Thailand against Texas, which is what cultural transmission predicts and what a divine relational strategy does not. The lament Psalms attest the experience of hiddenness. They do not explain why a loving God would allow honest seekers to die in the silence.
rationale: Contested. This is the strongest atheological argument after evil, it is aimed precisely at the deconvert's actual experience, and pretending it has a tidy answer will read as gaslighting to anyone who lived it. Lead by validating the seeker's experience as real and biblically attested, at Isaiah 45:15 and Psalm 13. Then offer Moser and Pascal as a coherent account of why a love-seeking God might not maximise obviousness — coherent, not conclusive. Never say 'they secretly resisted'.

plain.d: J. L. Schellenberg argues like this. A loving God would make himself available to anyone open to knowing him. But there are people who do not believe and are not resisting. They sought God in earnest, some through years of anguished prayer. They found silence.

plain.t: The first Christian response is to believe them
plain.d: Many who have left the faith are exhibit A here. Their seeking was real. "You secretly resisted" is unkind and unfounded. Never say it.

Paul Moser argues that God's aim is filial knowledge, meaning love that changes you, not spectator certainty. Evidence strong enough to force agreement without surrender might produce exactly the wrong relationship. Pascal saw the same asymmetry: "enough light for those who desire to see, enough obscurity for those of a contrary disposition." Scripture says the experience is real. "Truly, you are a God who hides himself" (Isaiah 45:15). A third of the Psalms lament the silence. The claim was never that God is obvious. It is that he is findable (Jeremiah 29:13).

Schellenberg's replies are strong. A relationship needs you to believe the other party is there. A loving parent does not hide so well the child doubts she has one. Whatever obscurity buys, an all-powerful God could buy it and still let you know he exists. The wrong-kind-of-belief worry confuses knowing God is real with surrendering to him. Contested. After the problem of evil, this is the strongest atheist argument going. It aims straight at the experience of someone who really tried. Pretending it has a tidy answer will land as gaslighting to anyone who lived it. So validate the seeking first. Then offer Moser and Pascal as a coherent account, not a proof.
"I believe you looked. I'm not going to tell you that you didn't."

title: The Canaanite commands: the real options, laid out without flinching
claim: The texts are as hard as skeptics say. Deuteronomy 20:16-18 and 1 Samuel 15, as written, command total destruction, including children. The faithful options each come with a price. (1) Ancient Near Eastern war rhetoric: 'utterly destroyed... left none remaining' was conventional hyperbole. Joshua 10-11 reports the total annihilation of cities whose inhabitants are alive and numerous chapters later in Judges 1, and other ANE victory texts brag identically about survivors — Merneptah's 'Israel is wasted, his seed is not'. Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan argue the commands target military strongholds and dispossession, not extermination. (2) The Bible's own dominant verb is 'drive out', gradually, 'little by little' (Exodus 23:29-30), after a 400-year moral forbearance (Genesis 15:16). (3) Archaeology's minimal-conquest picture, in which most sites show no destruction layer, ironically undercuts a literal genocide reading. (4) Then the hard views. Nicholas Wolterstorff reads the accounts as hagiographic hyperbole never meant literally. Others bite the bullet on divine prerogative. Still others, such as Eric Seibert and Peter Enns, say the texts reflect Israel's assumptions about God rather than God — a costly move for biblical authority. No option is free. Say which one you hold, and say its price.

sources.name: Paul Copan & Matthew Flannagan, Did God Really Command Genocide?
Nicholas Wolterstorff on reading Joshua (in Divine Evil?, OUP)
Wikipedia, 'The Bible and violence' (survey of positions)
Randal Rauser's internal critique (the honest in-house objection)

response: The steelmanned objection runs like this. 1 Samuel 15 is not siege rhetoric. Saul is condemned for insufficient killing, and 'infant and nursing child' is specified. Hyperbole readings look motivated, applied exactly and only where the morality is intolerable, and a hermeneutic elastic enough to soften genocide commands can soften anything — which forfeits the claim that the text constrains its readers. Raising the ban to 'dispossession' merely relabels ethnic cleansing. And then there is the internal critique, pressed by the Christian philosopher Randal Rauser as much as by atheists. If your moral perception is reliable enough to recognise the resurrection's God as good, it is reliable enough to recognise commanded infant-killing as evil. You cannot switch it off selectively when the text needs rescuing.
rationale: Contested, with no pretence otherwise. This is the hardest text-level objection Christianity faces, and the entry's value is showing the map honestly rather than selling one exit. Never quick-answer this in conversation. Acknowledge the horror first — the skeptic's moral reaction is functioning exactly as Romans 2 says it should. Then present the options with their costs. Evidential weight for the positive case is low. This is pure defence, and modelling honest defence is the point.

title: 'Then who made God?' — a category error, honestly scoped
claim: The popular version fails on the definitions. No classical theistic argument premises that everything has a cause. The Kalam says everything that begins has a cause. The contingency argument says every contingent thing needs an explanation. God, as classically defined, neither begins nor is contingent. A necessary being is precisely the kind of thing the question cannot apply to, so asking who made the unmade is asking what lies north of the North Pole. Dawkins's upgraded version — that a designing God would be even more complex, and hence more improbable — imports the assumption that God is a composite physical system whose complexity needs assembling. Classical theism denies exactly that, under the doctrine of divine simplicity, and Dawkins nowhere engages the actual doctrine; Edward Feser has written at length on the confusion. An honest scope note: there is a sophisticated version that survives. Graham Oppy asks why the initial physical state cannot be the necessary stopping point instead of God. That is a real question. But notice that it concedes this entry's point. Something must be uncaused and necessary, and the argument is over what. The schoolyard gotcha is dead. The grown-up debate is the contingency argument.

sources.name: SEP, 'Cosmological Argument' (what the premises actually say)
Edward Feser on the 'who made God' confusion
Richard Dawkins, The God Delusion ch. 4 (the Boeing 747 gambit)
SEP, 'Divine Simplicity'

response: The best skeptical salvage comes from Oppy, and from Russell before him. Fine: no serious argument says everything has a cause. But then the theist has abandoned the intuitive engine that made the argument feel forceful, and the naturalist simply claims the same exemption for the universe's initial state — necessary, uncaused, brute. Now both worldviews terminate in an unexplained necessary something, and the naturalist's candidate is one we already know exists, with no additional attributes such as omniscience or personhood purchased on credit. 'Why is God exempt?' fails. 'Why is God a better stopping point than physics?' does not. And divine simplicity, the doctrine doing the anti-Dawkins work, is itself contested even among theists.
rationale: Unrefuted. Against the popular objection as actually posed, the category answer stands, and even sophisticated atheists such as Oppy prosecute a different and better question instead. Answer the gotcha in two sentences, cheerfully concede that the real debate — which stopping point is better — is live, and route it to the Kalam and contingency entry. Do not spike the football. The person asking usually heard it from a YouTube short, and deserves the respectful version.

Asking who made the unmade is like asking what is north of the North Pole.

Richard Dawkins offers a better one in The God Delusion. A designing God would be even more complex, so even less likely. That assumes God is a built-up physical system that had to be assembled. Classical theism denies exactly that, under the name divine simplicity. Dawkins nowhere engages the doctrine. Edward Feser has written at length on the confusion.

But the theist has now given up the intuition that made the argument feel forceful. The naturalist claims the same exemption for the universe's first state. Necessary, uncaused, brute. Now both sides end in an unexplained something. And the naturalist's candidate is one we already know exists, with no extra traits bought on credit. Divine simplicity, the doctrine doing the work here, is also contested among theists.

Something must be uncaused. The argument is over what. That is the contingency argument, and it is live.

Answer in two sentences and move on. Concede cheerfully that the real debate is which stopping point is better. Do not spike the football. The person asking usually got it from a short video, and deserves the respectful version.
