title: Science and Genesis: Christianity is not married to a six-thousand-year-old earth
claim: The objection 'science has disproven Genesis, therefore Christianity is false' assumes that young-earth literalism is the Christian reading. It never was the only one. Augustine, writing On the Literal Meaning of Genesis around AD 415 — fourteen centuries before Darwin — argued that the 'days' need not be solar days, and warned that Christians talking scientific nonsense about the world, 'to the derision of unbelievers', disgrace the faith. Origen had earlier noted that days one through three occur before the sun exists, which signals the text's own non-literal cues. The current faithful range includes young-earth creationism, old-earth and day-age readings, the framework reading, John Walton's cosmic-temple reading in which Genesis 1 gives functional origins rather than material mechanics, and evolutionary creation as taught by BioLogos and by Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project while confessing the creeds. This site takes no position among them. The point is narrower and stronger. 'Evolution, therefore atheism' is a non sequitur on which young-earth fundamentalism and New Atheism strangely agree, since both insist that Genesis must be either a science textbook or a lie. The tradition's oldest readers knew better.

sources.name: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram (the 'derision of unbelievers' passage, I.19)
BioLogos (Francis Collins's organization)
John Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One
American Scientific Affiliation (spectrum of Christian views)

response: The skeptic presses back. The range of readings is real, but its timing is suspicious. Softer readings surged just when geology and Darwin made a literal one untenable. That looks like a retreat dressed as exegesis. And Augustine aside, the usual premodern reading was a young earth and a global flood. The problem also runs past chapter one. An evolved history means no first-couple bottleneck, on the genetics of populations. That strains the historical Adam, the Fall, and Paul's Adam-Christ architecture in Romans 5. Dennett's 'universal acid' eats more than the six days. At some point, says the skeptic, rewriting under fire looks just like a theory that can absorb any evidence against it.
rationale: Unrefuted for the narrow claim actually made. 'Science falsifies Christianity' fails, because the softer readings are ancient. Augustine and Origen predate geology by over a thousand years, and the after-the-fact charge breaks on that fact. Christianity's core claims are about Christ, not chronology. The honest limits: the historical Adam and the Fall are genuinely hard theological work in progress, and you should grant that. Never let a talk about God become a young-earth referendum. The site must not marry that position.

title: 'Religion causes all wars' — the data says otherwise; use it with clean hands
claim: The Encyclopedia of Wars, by Phillips and Axelrod, is a standard secular reference cataloguing 1,763 wars across recorded history. It classifies 123 of them — about 7% — as having religious causes. The overwhelming drivers of war are territory, resources, dynastic succession and power: the ordinary appetites of states. The twentieth century sharpens the point, since history's largest body counts accrued under regimes that were explicitly anti-religious — Stalin's USSR, Mao's China, Pol Pot's Cambodia. Now the discipline required in using this. The conclusion is not 'atheism causes gulags'. That would be the mirror image of the fallacy being answered, and unfair to the atheist neighbour for exactly the reasons that 'religion causes wars' is unfair to the believer. The conclusion is narrower and biblical. Removing religion demonstrably does not remove atrocity, because the common variable is human beings plus unaccountable power — which is roughly what the doctrine of sin has claimed all along (Jeremiah 17:9). Religion has been a real accelerant in real wars, and Christians should say so about the Crusades and the Thirty Years' War without flinching. But the causal arrow 'no religion, therefore peace' is empirically dead.

sources.name: Phillips & Axelrod, Encyclopedia of Wars (the 123/1763 classification)
Wikipedia, 'Religious war' (data and debate)
The Black Book of Communism (20th-century state atrocity counts)
David Bentley Hart, Atheist Delusions (historical corrective)

response: The skeptic's better version starts with classification. The 7% figure depends on how you sort, and religion is entangled with 'political' wars everywhere. Was the Thirty Years' War dynastic or confessional? Yes. Hitchens's actual thesis was never that religion causes all wars, but that religion poisons the conflicts it touches, supplying absolute stakes, out-group sanctification and divine permission. As for the atheist-state rebuttal, those regimes functioned as quasi-religions, with infallible doctrine, sacred texts and heresy trials. So they arguably indict dogmatic certainty rather than secularism — though the theist may fairly note that this rescue risks special pleading in both directions, since defining every atrocity as 'religious in structure' makes the claim unfalsifiable.
rationale: Unrefuted against the claim as popularly made, that religion is the main cause of war. The data is secular and decisive. The usage discipline is the whole game. Concede religious atrocities specifically and by name. Never weaponise Stalin as 'atheism did it'. Frame the twentieth century as proof that secularism does not fix humans, which is an argument for the doctrine of sin, not an argument against your neighbour. Used clean, this flips a gotcha into common ground about human nature; David Bentley Hart's Atheist Delusions is the long-form corrective.

plain.d: The Encyclopedia of Wars, by Phillips and Axelrod, is a standard secular work. It lists 1,763 wars across all of recorded history. It counts 123 of them as having religious causes. That is about 7%. The rest were fought over land, goods, thrones and power. Those are the plain wants of states, and they have not changed.
The largest death tolls in history came under regimes that were openly anti-religious. Stalin's Soviet Union. Mao's China. Pol Pot's Cambodia. The Black Book of Communism collects the counts.

The conclusion is not that atheism causes gulags. That is the same error in a mirror. It is unfair to your atheist neighbour for the same reasons. The point is narrower. Take away faith and you do not take away atrocity. What stays constant is people plus power with no check on it. That is roughly what the doctrine of sin has said all along (Jeremiah 17:9). Faith has been a real accelerant in real wars. Say so about the Crusades, the Inquisition and the Thirty Years' War, and do not flinch.

The 7% depends on how you sort. Faith is tangled into political wars everywhere. Was the Thirty Years' War dynastic or confessional? Yes. Christopher Hitchens never claimed that religion causes all wars. His claim was that it poisons the fights it touches. It hands out absolute stakes, holy enemies and divine permission. As for the atheist states, they ran like churches. Fixed doctrine, sacred texts, trials for heresy. So they may indict blind certainty rather than the lack of a god. Though if every atrocity counts as religious in shape, the claim can never be tested. That risk cuts both ways.

Strong, against the claim as people actually make it. The data is secular and it is clear. But the care you take in using it is the whole game. Name the Christian atrocities, one by one. Never use Stalin as a weapon. Frame the last century as proof that dropping God does not fix people. That argues for the doctrine of sin, not against your neighbour. David Bentley Hart's Atheist Delusions is the long version.
"Taking religion away didn't make the twentieth century gentle. I think the problem is us."

title: The banana and 'just look at the trees': retire the design shortcut
claim: Ray Comfort's 2006 argument that the banana is 'the atheist's nightmare' — perfectly shaped for the human hand, with a tab at the top and a biodegradable wrapper — failed in the most instructive way possible. The Cavendish banana is a seedless cultivar produced by centuries of human selective breeding. Wild bananas are stubby, seed-packed and barely edible. The argument accidentally credited God's design to agronomists, and it lives on as a joke format in atheist spaces. Its gentler cousin, 'how can you see the trees and not believe?', is not wrong as testimony. Psalm 19 and Romans 1:20 describe a real perception of glory through creation. But testimony is not argument. Offered as an argument, it invites the immediate counter that Darwin himself felt: look also at the Ichneumonidae, whose larvae eat caterpillars alive, and at childhood cancers, and at the parasites of the eye. If the design intuition is worth defending in argument form — and it is — then the defensible version is fine-tuning, which survives expert scrutiny. The banana does not.

SEP, 'Teleological Arguments' (what a serious design argument looks like)

response: The skeptic's rebuttal is simply correct. The banana was designed, by humans, via artificial selection — which is precisely the naturalistic mechanism writ small. And appeals to everyday biological 'perfection' collapse under dysteleology: the recurrent laryngeal nerve's detour, the vertebrate blind spot, parasitic life cycles. Comfort himself later conceded the banana point. 'Look at the trees' proves the speaker's experience of wonder, which the atheist may share while attributing it to deep time and selection. It moves no one who does not already believe.
rationale: Don't use. The skeptical counter is right on the facts, and deploying refuted arguments taxes the credibility of every good argument you make afterwards. Redirect instead. The wonder is legitimate as testimony — say 'this is what the world looks like to me', honestly. But the argument-form belongs to fine-tuning, where the numbers are real and the interlocutors are physicists.

title: 'No transitional fossils' and the second law of thermodynamics: bad science, bad witness
claim: Two arguments to retire together, plainly. First: 'there are no transitional fossils' is false — not disputed, false. Tiktaalik is a fish-tetrapod intermediate that was found by predicting which rock stratum and age to search. Archaeopteryx exists. So does the therapsid reptile-mammal sequence, the whale series from Pakicetus through Ambulocetus to Basilosaurus, and the hominin fossil record. They are displayed in museums, and in an important sense every fossil population is transitional. Second: 'evolution violates the second law of thermodynamics' misuses physics. The second law governs closed systems, and Earth is not one. It receives a torrent of low-entropy sunlight, and local increases in order are utterly routine — an embryo, a snowflake, a refrigerator — while total entropy still rises. Even major creationist organisations now list versions of these arguments among those to avoid. The deeper issue is Augustine's, sixteen centuries old. A Christian talking demonstrable nonsense about nature, 'to the derision of unbelievers', teaches the unbeliever that the faith itself is nonsense. Whatever position one takes on origins, it must not be defended with claims that a first-year biology or physics student can refute.

TalkOrigins CF001: second law claims
Answers in Genesis, 'Arguments to Avoid' (creationists policing their own)

response: The skeptical rebuttal is settled science, not opinion. The transitional series are catalogued, physical and public, and Tiktaalik was a successful prediction of evolutionary theory — the strongest kind of evidence there is. The thermodynamics claim fails on the first page of any textbook treatment, since open systems importing energy decrease local entropy constantly. A skeptic who hears these arguments concludes, reasonably, that the speaker either does not understand the science or does not care. He then files everything else the speaker says, including the resurrection case, under the same heading.

Christians hold a range of origins views, as the science-and-Genesis entry sets out. None of those views needs, or is helped by, claims that are simply wrong. The cost is paid by the Gospel's credibility, exactly as Augustine warned.

title: 'Darwin recanted on his deathbed': the Lady Hope legend is false
claim: The story that Charles Darwin renounced evolution and embraced Christ on his deathbed traces to 'Lady Hope', Elizabeth Hope, a British evangelist. She told a Massachusetts gathering in 1915 — thirty-three years after Darwin died in 1882 — that she had visited him near the end and found him reading Hebrews and lamenting his theory. Darwin's family, who were actually present at his death, flatly denied it. His daughter Henrietta Litchfield wrote in print in 1922: 'I was present at his deathbed... He never recanted any of his scientific views, then or earlier.' Darwin died an agnostic, courteous toward a faith he did not share, and no serious historian — Christian or otherwise — credits the tale. Notice also that the story would prove nothing even if it were true. Theories stand or fall on evidence, not on their authors' final anxieties. Christianity would not be falsified by a deathbed recantation from Paul's biographer, and evolution is not falsified by one from Darwin. Repeating this legend does double damage: it spreads a falsehood, and it implies that the speaker's case needs one.

The skeptic is right, the historians are right, and even the major creationist organisations agree the story is false — Answers in Genesis lists it among arguments to avoid, and James Moore's The Darwin Legend is the scholarly autopsy. The Darwin family's firsthand denials, the thirty-three-year gap, and the total absence of corroboration settle it. A Christian repeating it is bearing false witness about a dead man, in service of a point that would be logically worthless even if the story were true.
rationale: Don't use, ever. The command against false witness does not have an apologetics exemption. If it comes up, the Christian's move is to debunk it first. Nothing builds trust with a skeptic faster than watching a believer kill a convenient legend on principle.

"That story isn't true. His daughter denied it in print, and I'm not going to repeat it."

title: Pascal's wager as an opener: wrong tool, wrong slot
claim: Deployed as a conversation-opener — 'you might as well believe; if you're wrong you lose nothing' — the wager fails three ways, and skeptics know all three. The many-gods objection: the same bet works for Allah, for Vishnu, or for a deity who rewards honest doubt and punishes hedged belief, so the wager alone selects no religion. The doxastic problem: belief is not a light switch, and no one can sincerely believe a proposition for prize money — as the skeptic being lectured is vividly aware while not believing. The mercenary problem: it presents faith as fire insurance, which misrepresents a Gospel whose call is love of God, not actuarial self-interest. What almost everyone misses is that Pascal knew all this. The wager appears in the Pensées at fragment 233, aimed at a specific reader: the sophisticated Parisian too indifferent to investigate. Its real function is anti-apathy — to show that the God question is not intellectually optional, and that the stakes make honest investigation mandatory. After that, Pascal prescribes practice and inquiry, not instant belief. That limited use survives, as a closing nudge to a genuine inquirer, not as an opening argument to a skeptic.

response: The skeptic's objections are sound against the popular version. The wager is decision theory with a rigged partition, since it assumes exactly two live options. It demands belief as an act of will, which is impossible. And the God it imagines — one fooled by self-interested compliance — is not worth believing in, since an omniscient being would presumably prefer honest disbelief to strategic pretence. Even the rehabilitated anti-apathy use has a limit. It motivates inquiry, and inquiry may honestly conclude against faith. The wager cannot then be re-invoked to overrule the verdict it commissioned.
rationale: Don't use as an opener or as a proof. It is graded 'answered' because in its common street form the skeptical counters succeed. The salvage is real, and Peter Kreeft has reconstructed it sympathetically. At the end of a conversation with a genuinely undecided person, Pascal's actual point — that this question is too important for indifference, so investigate it seriously — is both honest and effective. Slot matters: last word to the apathetic, never first word to the skeptic.

Peter Kreeft has reconstructed that limited use sympathetically.

Slot matters. Last word to someone apathetic. Never first word to a skeptic. The salvage is real. At the end of a talk with a genuinely undecided person, Pascal's actual point stands. This question is too important to be indifferent about.
"I'm not asking you to bet. I'm asking whether the question is worth your serious attention."

title: Mind-reading the atheist: 'you secretly believe,' 'you have no morals,' 'atheism takes more faith'
claim: Three tropes to retire, and Scripture itself retires the worst of them. 'Atheists secretly believe and are suppressing it' proof-texts Romans 1 while ignoring Romans 2:14-15, where Gentiles without the law 'do by nature what the law requires' because it is 'written on their hearts'. The Bible predicts morally serious, conscience-driven unbelievers. It does not license telling your neighbour that she is lying about her own inner life. Empirically, many atheists are deconverts who describe leaving faith as painful, slow and honest, often by way of church hurt — John Marriott's research documents exactly that. Telling them their loss was secretly insincere reopens the wound and ends the conversation. 'Atheists have no basis for morality' conflates a legitimate metaethical question, about what grounds moral facts, with a slander that atheists are not moral — false in observation and, per Romans 2, false in doctrine. 'It takes more faith to be an atheist' equivocates, since the atheist means by 'faith' precisely what she rejects, so the line lands as a taunt rather than an argument. All three substitute diagnosis of the person for engagement with the position. The entire posture of this section depends on refusing that substitution.

I left slowly, honestly, and at real personal cost, and being told otherwise is being called a liar.' On morality: moral motivation and moral knowledge are demonstrably independent of metaethics. Atheists donate kidneys and run soup kitchens, and Euthyphro-style questions show that grounding puzzles cut at theists too. On 'more faith': defining the atheist's evidential standard as 'faith' is a word game that concedes the argument by changing the dictionary. Each rebuttal is correct, and each trope, when deployed, confirms the deconvert's suspicion that the church argues in bad faith.
rationale: Don't use. It is graded 'answered' because the skeptical rebuttals to all three tropes succeed, and in this case the Bible is on the skeptic's side of the exchange, since Romans 2 predicts the moral atheist. Engage arguments, never diagnose interlocutors. With deconverts especially, ask about their story before offering any case at all. This entry is the tonal keystone of the whole section.

plain.d: "You secretly believe, and you're suppressing it." "You have no basis for morality." "Atheism takes more faith than Christianity." All three are common. All three should go.

It proof-texts Romans 1 and skips Romans 2:14-15, where Gentiles without the law "do by nature what the law requires" because it is "written on their hearts." The Bible predicts morally serious unbelievers. It does not license telling your neighbour she is lying about her own inner life.

Many atheists are deconverts. They describe leaving as slow, painful and honest, and it often began with being hurt by a church. John Marriott has researched exactly that. Telling them the loss was secretly insincere reopens the wound and ends the conversation.

"No basis for morality" mixes a real question with a slander. The real question is what grounds moral facts, and that is the moral argument, worth having. The slander is that atheists are not moral. That is false in observation and false in doctrine, per Romans 2. "It takes more faith" is a word game. The atheist means by faith precisely the thing she rejects, so the line lands as a taunt, not an argument.

plain.t: Do not use any of them

Engage arguments. Never diagnose people. With deconverts especially, ask about their story before you offer any case at all. The rest of this section depends on that one habit.
"What happened? I'd rather hear your story than argue with a version of you I invented."

title: 'They died for it' — the argument in the only form that works
claim: The disciples suffered, and in several cases died, rather than deny that they had seen Jesus alive. People will die for something they sincerely believe. Nobody dies for something they know they made up. And these particular people were in a position to know.
response: The skeptic's reply comes in three parts, and the first two are right. (1) Sincerity proves nothing about truth. The 9/11 hijackers died for their faith, as have Heaven's Gate members, Jim Jones's congregation, and martyrs of every religion on earth. Willingness to die establishes that a person believes what they are saying, and nothing more. (2) The historical record for most of the apostles is very thin. Only one apostolic death is recorded in the New Testament: James son of Zebedee, beheaded by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). The vivid traditions — Thomas speared in India, Bartholomew flayed alive, Andrew on an X-shaped cross, Peter crucified upside down — come from apocryphal Acts written between the second and fourth centuries, which also contain talking animals and resurrected fish. Sean McDowell's The Fate of the Apostles (2015) is the most thorough treatment by a Christian scholar, and he grades the evidence honestly. He judges the martyrdoms of Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee and James the brother of Jesus to be historically well-established, John's death to be probably natural, and most of the rest to be possible but not demonstrable. (3) And even granting all of it, martyrdom establishes only that the disciples sincerely believed they had seen the risen Jesus — which skeptical scholars like Gerd Lüdemann already concede without difficulty, explaining the belief as visionary experience.

rationale: Graded contested, because the popular version fails and the disciplined version holds, and the difference between them is everything. What survives scrutiny is a narrow, real point. The disciples were not in the position of ordinary religious martyrs. A Muslim martyr dies for a revelation he received on someone else's testimony. A Heaven's Gate member dies for a metaphysics nobody could check. The disciples are claiming to have eaten with a man they watched die — a claim about which they personally could not be honestly mistaken in the way a second-hand believer can. Either they saw something, or they knew they had not. Paul is the sharpest case, because he was persecuting the movement and had every worldly reason not to join it, and 2 Corinthians 11 lists what it cost him, in his own hand. So the argument does real work, but bounded work. It establishes sincerity, not truth. It rules out deliberate fraud — the 'they stole the body and made it up' theory — and it rules out nothing else. Present it that way, with the thin evidence for the ten conceded up front, and it is durable. Present it as 'all twelve apostles were tortured to death and none recanted' and you will meet someone who has read McDowell, or Candida Moss's The Myth of Persecution, and you will lose everything you said before it.
talk: Never say 'all twelve were martyred.' Say the narrow thing: **“I'm not arguing that dying for a belief makes it true — plenty of people have died for things that were false. I'm arguing these particular men were in a position to know whether they had made it up, and they behaved for the rest of their lives like men who hadn't.”** Then concede the evidence for most of them is late and thin, and name Paul, who was on the other side first.

plain.d: The disciples suffered, and some of them died, rather than deny that they had seen Jesus alive. People will die for what they truly believe. Nobody dies for a thing they know they made up. And these men were in a place to know.

plain.t: Two thirds of the reply are right

Those come from the apocryphal Acts, written between the second and fourth centuries. Those same texts have talking animals and a smoked fish brought back to life. Sean McDowell's The Fate of the Apostles (Routledge, 2015) is the fullest Christian study, and he grades the evidence honestly. "They weren't taking someone's word for it. They said they ate with a man they had watched die."

title: DON'T USE: 'all twelve apostles were martyred and not one recanted'
claim: A staple of sermons and tracts. Every one of the twelve was tortured to death. A single recantation would have ended Christianity, yet not one of them broke.
response: There is no ancient source that says this, and there never was. The New Testament records one apostolic death, James son of Zebedee (Acts 12:2). Peter and Paul's deaths in Rome are early and well-attested. 1 Clement, written around AD 95, speaks of their sufferings, and Tacitus describes Nero's persecution. But the specific details, including the upside-down cross, come from later tradition. For most of the others, the source is a body of apocryphal Acts composed from the second to the fourth century. Those same texts feature a talking lion and a resurrected smoked fish. Early Christian tradition holds that John died of old age at Ephesus, which Eusebius reports in Church History 3.31. That by itself falsifies the 'all twelve' claim. The 'not one recanted' half is worse. It argues from the absence of records nobody kept. We have no roster of who held firm, because we have no reliable roster of what happened to most of them at all. Sean McDowell wrote as a Christian apologist, specifically to defend this line of evidence. He is the one who documents how little of it can be established.

rationale: Avoid it. It overclaims a real argument into a false one, and the correction is a single search away. The moment a skeptic checks Thomas or Bartholomew and finds a third-century romance, everything true you said about the crucifixion, the creed and Paul is suspect. You have taught them that you repeat things you have not checked. The fix is not to drop the evidence. Shrink the claim to what the sources carry: Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee and James the brother of Jesus. The last of those is attested by Josephus, who was not a Christian. Four well-documented deaths, made in the strongest possible position of knowledge, is a better argument than twelve legendary ones. It is better precisely because it survives being checked.
talk: If you have used this one — and most of us have — say so: **“I used to say all twelve were martyred. That's not what the sources support, and I stopped saying it.”** Then give the four that hold. Nothing rebuilds credibility with a skeptic faster than a Christian correcting a Christian talking point unprompted.
